Five familiar situations where your intuition is almost certainly doing the math wrong.

01Shared birthdays

How many people before a shared birthday is more likely than not?

You do not need hundreds. You barely need a classroom.

MAY01MAY06MAY12MAY19MAY21MAY07MAY15MAY21MAY24MAY29MAY03MAY11MAY17MAY30MAY05

50.7%

Chance two of 23 people share a birthday

With 23 people there are 253 possible pairs that could match. The useful shortcut is to calculate the chance that every birthday is different, then subtract that result from one.

1 − ∏(365 − k) / 365, k = 0 → 22

02Chain of relationships

How many introductions separate two strangers?

A huge network can still feel surprisingly small.

AlexSam

≈ 6

The famous average path length is small—not magic

There is no fixed answer for every network. Researchers compare the shortest paths between pairs of people; a few highly connected people create shortcuts that pull the average down dramatically.

Average the shortest path between every pair

03Guessing a password

What does one extra character really add?

Not one more guess. An entire new layer of possibilities.

A7KQ0Z2ML3NB8PY4DXQ1R6T9C

218,340,105,584,896

62 characters across eight positions

Each position can contain any of 62 letters or numbers, so every added position multiplies the whole possibility space by 62. This counts combinations; it does not model how real password attacks work.

62⁸ = 218,340,105,584,896

04Green lights in a row

What are the odds of hitting five greens in a row?

Even friendly odds become unforgiving when every light has to cooperate.

Five independent 50% green lights

3.125%

One perfect run in every 32 attempts

If each light were independently green half the time, five greens means multiplying one-half by itself five times. Real traffic signals are coordinated, so this is a deliberately simple model rather than a prediction for a route.

(1 / 2)⁵ = 1 / 32 = 3.125%

05Monty Hall

A losing door opens. Should you stay or switch?

The host knows where the prize is, so the reveal changes what the remaining door means.

123

66.7%

Chance of winning when you switch

Your first choice has a one-in-three chance. The other two doors share the remaining two-in-three chance; after the host knowingly removes a losing door, that probability sits with the one unopened alternative.

Stay: 1 / 3  ·  Switch: 2 / 3

Chance looks different when it moves.

Probability is not always intuitive. That is why it is worth making visible.
